title: Every Change Is an Event: Event-Driven Listing Architecture
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, acceptance criteria AC-1 to AC-3, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the event-driven-listings entry in journal-spec.json. Four units are additions to the published text: the lead-ins to the trade-off table (p54) and the vertical table (p57), and the conclusion's synthesis (p68); p03 gains a roadmap sentence and p21 a gloss of 'tenant'. See decision_log.

know: The difference between domain events, change events and commands; notification, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing; ordering, delivery guarantees and idempotency.

The listing event stream: components, the transactional outbox, change data capture behind a translator during migration, the event envelope (listing key, aggregate version, cause, public state), the event catalog, topics and retention.

Schema evolution under compatibility modes and the rules Veldmark publishes; replay, backfills and dead letters that cannot resurrect a sold listing; removal objectives separate from publication objectives.
believe: The listing event is a published contract with one owner, not an integration detail, and change data capture is a source, not a contract.
Reliable publication and safe consumption are two halves, and neither alone gives correct downstream state.
can_do: Review a listing event design and say what goes wrong at the weekly peak, during a backfill or after a schema change.

Decide which parts of the event contract a group sets centrally and which each brand keeps.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a stale downstream copy and a replay plan, the reader names the mechanism that fixes each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A listing sells at 18:10 and leaves search at 18:11, but the next morning's alert digest, built the afternoon before from a database replica, still features it. Separately, a team plans to rebuild the search index by replaying six months of listing events and fears that old events will bring sold listings back. Using only this chapter: what design fixes the digest, and what makes the replay safe?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One owned listing event stream emitted by the system of record through an outbox (or CDC behind a translator), to which the digest subscribes, so ListingSold removes the bike; and a derived artifact that re-checks listing state at send time. Consumers apply events only when the per-listing version is higher than the one they hold, events carry current public state, and the replay reads a compacted state topic where sold listings end in tombstones, so no old event resurrects a sold listing.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A listing written once and read by ten or twenty systems, so the question is how changes move, not how they are stored; one published stream replacing private integrations; the chapter opening Part VII and owning the listing event, outbox and schema evolution, with copies and tracking left to the next chapters. Then the bike incident at Veldmark, event concepts, the stream's architecture, public evidence and Listing event contract v1, schema evolution, replay and dead letters, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: dated classifieds engineering sources (Adevinta, Kleinanzeigen, Vinted, AutoScout24, mobile.de), Confluent and Debezium documentation, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.
Given a proposal to publish after commit or to let consumers read raw change data capture, the reader names what breaks and the two designs that fix it, with their costs.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A listing service commits a sale to its database and then sends a Kafka message from application code. Separately, the search and alert teams, tired of waiting, want to read Debezium change events from the monolith's listing table directly. Using only this chapter: what can go wrong in each case, and what should be built instead, at what cost?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A crash between commit and publish leaves the listing sold in the database and active everywhere else (and publishing first leaves consumers believing a change that never committed): the dual-write problem. A transactional outbox writes the event in the same transaction and a relay publishes it, at the cost of a write-path change, an extra table and at-least-once delivery. Raw change events make the producer's internal schema a public contract, so a column rename breaks every consumer; change data capture is allowed only as a source behind a translator (an anti-corruption layer) that emits the contract events, until the new service publishes the same contract through its own outbox.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two schema changes, the reader says which the registry catches, which it cannot, and how each is made.
acceptance_criteria.probe: On a listing event topic with many consumers, one brand wants to rename a field, and another wants to start sending a surface-area field as habitable surface instead of total surface. Using only this chapter: how should each change be made, and which of them would a schema registry stop?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Under full transitive compatibility only optional fields with defaults can be added or removed; a rename is done by adding the new field, populating both, deprecating the old one and removing it in a new major version (v2, by parallel run on a new topic). A change of meaning passes every registry check because the registry checks syntax, not semantics, so it is never made in place: it gets a new field with a new name, and every change is reviewed by people (at Veldmark, the advice forum's one-week event-catalog review).

acceptance_criteria.statement: No real company's internal listing event design is presented as fact; company evidence is dated and inferences are labeled.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Does the chapter describe any real company's listing event names, topics or consumer logic as documented fact beyond what its cited, dated sources say? Is every inference about a real company labeled as the author's?

The dual-write problem and the transactional outbox; change data capture behind a translator.

thesis.question: How should listing changes flow to search, trust, alerts, analytics and partners?
thesis.claim: Listing changes should reach search, alerts, trust and safety, SEO, analytics and partners through one owned, versioned stream of listing events that only the listing's system of record emits: published in the same transaction as the change (a transactional outbox, or change data capture behind a translator while a monolith remains), keyed by listing ID with a strictly increasing per-listing version that consumers use to apply each change once and in order, carrying the listing's current public state so a consumer recovers from a lost message with the next one, evolved under full transitive schema compatibility with semantic changes reviewed by people, replayable from a compacted state topic, and held to a removal objective tighter than the publication objective (at Veldmark p99 under five seconds to topic and under thirty seconds to search deletion).
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of letting each downstream system poll the listing database or a replica, receive nightly dumps or messages the application sends after commit, or read change-data-capture rows as its contract, with each producing team choosing its own event names and payloads.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this decides centrally the envelope, the cross-brand listing identity, the event catalog, the compatibility rules, the removal service levels and per-topic access, and leaves each brand its internal events and its choice of outbox or CDC during migration; makes consumers register before they get access; and watches publication and end-to-end removal latency per tenant, consumer lag at the Sunday-evening peak and the count of consumers still reading producer tables.
thesis.how_why: Femke's bike sold at 18:10 and left Solr at 18:11, but the next morning's digest, assembled from a MySQL replica the afternoon before, still featured it, and three people messaged her. Tradeyard NL alone had eleven readers of listing changes on five mechanisms, and nobody had the list. Replayed on Listing event contract v1, the ListingSold event at version 9 reaches the digest, which also re-checks state at send time. The contract went live on 1 July 2027 with 23 consumer groups and by the end of 2027 carried about 4.2 million events a day; content-hash suppression keeps about a million no-op updates a day off the stream. The Essen Golf's removal, reported by the dealer's feed 26 hours late, shows the limit: the stream makes copies as fresh as the source, not fresher.

supporting_claims.claim: Listing changes are a fan-out problem: one write has ten or twenty readers, and private integrations (polling, replica reads, nightly dumps, best-effort messages) leave nobody with the list of readers, so removals arrive late; the fix is a listing event defined as a domain event in the listing's published language, owned by its context, which change data capture can feed but never replace.

Reliable publication means only the listing's system of record emits listing events, in the same transaction as the change: a transactional outbox as the target, change data capture behind a translator while a monolith remains, the two being stages of one migration rather than alternatives.

Safe consumption needs a per-listing key and a strictly increasing per-listing version that consumers use to apply each change once and in order, and events that carry the listing's current public state plus the delta (no personal data), so a lost, duplicated or failed message is repaired by the next one.

A contract that lives for years needs full transitive schema compatibility with human review of changes in meaning, breaking changes by parallel run, replay from a compacted state topic and a separate backfill topic gated by version so no replay resurrects a sold listing, and a removal objective tighter than the publication objective (at Veldmark, p99 under five seconds to topic and under thirty seconds to search deletion, against p95 under two seconds for publication).

Veldmark's Listing event contract v1 shows the design working and its limit: replayed on v1, the bike's ListingSold at version 9 reaches the digest, which also re-checks state at send time, while the Essen Golf's 26-hour-late removal shows the stream makes copies only as fresh as their source.

Because the contract outlives the systems around it, a Chief Architect sets centrally the envelope, cross-brand identity, event catalog, compatibility rules, removal service levels and per-topic access, leaves brands their internal events and their outbox-or-CDC choice during migration, makes consumers register before access, and watches publication and removal latency, peak lag and consumers still reading producer tables.

role.contribution: Publishes the first platform contract, the listing event stream, that every later chapter of the part reads from.

flow.rationale: The scene poses the question with a sold bike that a digest never heard about; concepts give the vocabulary (domain event, state transfer, key, version) the architecture needs; the architecture builds publication, envelope, catalog and topics from it; the in-practice section can then test the design on public evidence and on the bike and the Golf; schema evolution and replay come after the contract exists, because they govern how it changes and how its events are re-delivered; the judging sections generalize. Putting replay before the envelope would ask the reader to version-gate events before knowing they carry a version; putting the bike replay before the architecture would show a fix before its parts.

hook.content: A listing is written by one party and read by many. The seller or a dealer's feed changes the price once; search must re-index it, saved-search alerts must decide whether to notify watchers, the market-value model must re-score it, the trust-and-safety system must check whether the change is suspicious, the sitemap must update lastmod, the warehouse must record it, and a partner syndication feed may need to carry it.

bridge.from_reader_world: Architects whose marketplaces already move listing changes by polling, replica reads, nightly dumps and messages sent after commit, and who have just finished Parts IV to VI, which assumed those changes arrive.
bridge.to_topic: Moving listing changes as one owned, published stream, the first platform contract of Part VII.

thesis_statement.text: The listing event is a published contract with one owner; reliable publication (outbox, or change data capture behind a translator) and safe consumption (key, version, state) are two halves, and neither alone gives correct downstream state; carrying state and keeping history replayable turns rebuilds into routine operations.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing is written by one party and read by many systems, so the architecture question is not how to store the listing but how to move its changes, because that movement decides freshness, removal latency and consistency.

sections.heading: Concepts: What a Listing Event Is
sections.controlling_idea: A listing event is a domain event owned by the listing context, carrying state, keyed and versioned per listing, and it differs from change events, commands and thin notifications in who controls its shape.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the listing event as a contract and the ordering, delivery and idempotency properties consumers rely on.

flow.rationale: What kind of event (ownership) comes first because it decides who may change the shape; what the event carries (state) next because the envelope depends on it; how it is delivered (order, duplicates, versions) last because version-gated apply assumes events carry a version and the key.

transition_in.carries_over: The forum's question and the contract that answers it.
transition_in.introduces: The terms the contract is built from, starting with what counts as an event.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three things are called events (domain events, change events and commands), and the difference matters because it decides who controls their shape.

evidence.what: Domain event, change event (CDC) and command or message, with definition, who decides the shape, and an example of each.
evidence.shows: Shows that only a domain event's shape is set by the owning domain as a contract.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing event is a domain event about one listing, emitted by the owning context whenever the aggregate passes an invariant-preserving transition, and it serves as the aggregate's published language.

evidence.what: Transitions submitted, published, updated, price changed, paused, reserved, sold, expired, removed; published language as defined in bounded-contexts.
evidence.shows: Ties the event to the lifecycle readers already know and to the vocabulary other contexts use.

transition_in.carries_over: The three kinds of event.
transition_in.introduces: The book's definition of a listing event as a domain event.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Change data capture is a mechanism for getting events out of a legacy system, not a contract, because raw table changes make the producer's internal schema everybody's business.

evidence.what: Renaming a column in Yardstick should concern Daan Visser's team only; if eleven consumers parse the binlog of the ads table, it concerns everybody.
evidence.shows: Shows how reading raw changes couples consumers to the producer's internals.

transition_in.carries_over: The listing event as a domain event owned by the listing context.
transition_in.introduces: Change data capture, which looks similar but is a mechanism, not a contract.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Fowler separates event notification, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing, which trade payload size and privacy against callbacks, copies and the system of record.

evidence.what: Martin Fowler, 'What do you mean by "Event-Driven"?' (2017): notification makes consumers call back and hides the logical flow; state transfer means 'lots of data schlepped around and lots of copies'; event sourcing makes events the system of record, rarely worth it for listings.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the three options the next paragraph chooses between.

transition_in.carries_over: What kind of event a listing event is.
transition_in.introduces: What it should carry: Fowler's three patterns.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Listing events should carry state, because one popular change fans out to many readers at once and callbacks at the Sunday-evening peak would overload the listing service; which state is the envelope's question.

evidence.what: A price cut reaches search, alerts, valuation and analytics within seconds; a callback storm at peak.
evidence.shows: Explains why state transfer suits listings better than notification.

transition_in.carries_over: Fowler's three patterns and their costs.
transition_in.introduces: The choice for listings and why.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Consumers end up correct only through three properties: per-listing order from keying by listing ID, at-least-once delivery, and idempotency by version-gated apply.

evidence.what: Kafka order within a partition; Debezium's outbox router keys by aggregate ID, 'which preserves per-aggregate order'.
evidence.shows: Grounds per-listing ordering in the documented behaviour of the tools.

evidence.what: No end-to-end exactly-once across database, broker and search index; a consumer applies an event only if its version is newer than the one stored.
evidence.shows: Shows why duplicates must be expected and how a version makes them harmless.

transition_in.carries_over: What a listing event carries.
transition_in.introduces: How it is delivered and how consumers stay correct.

sections.heading: Architecture: The Listing Event Stream
sections.controlling_idea: The stream has five components with one owner each; the outbox or a CDC translator guarantees publication, a shared envelope with key, version, cause and public state makes consumption safe, a short catalog limits the contract, two topics let consumers catch up or bootstrap, and removals get a tighter objective than publications.

advances_thesis.how: Specifies how publication is guaranteed, what the envelope, catalog and topics give consumers, and how fast removals must arrive.

flow.rationale: Components first so each later part has an owner; publication (outbox, then CDC as the legacy path) before the envelope, because the envelope's fields are written by the publication mechanism; the envelope before the catalog because every event type shares it; topics next because retention and compaction depend on the state block and the event types; the removal objective last, because it measures how fast the closures the topics carry must arrive.

transition_in.carries_over: The concepts: domain events, state transfer, order, duplicates and versions.
transition_in.introduces: The architecture that puts them to work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The architecture has five parts, each with one owner, and only the listing context produces listing events, so trust and safety emits a decision the listing context applies rather than a listing event of its own.

evidence.what: Figure 2: one producer, one contract, many consumers; outbox, domain-event topic and compacted state topic.
evidence.shows: Shows publication as part of the write and the state topic serving consumers built later.

evidence.what: Listing context, publication mechanism, event backbone, schema registry, consumers.
evidence.shows: Gives each concern of the stream a single owner.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Publishing after a commit, or before it, creates the dual-write problem: a crash between the two steps leaves the database and every other copy disagreeing.

evidence.what: Commit then publish: listing sold in the database, active everywhere else, the bike's outcome from a different cause; publish then commit: consumers believe a change that never happened.
evidence.shows: Shows why neither order of two separate writes is safe.

transition_in.carries_over: The publication mechanism, the second component.
transition_in.introduces: The problem it must solve: the dual write.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The transactional outbox writes the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the change, and a relay publishes the rows, so a committed change cannot lose its event.

evidence.what: Debezium outbox event router: id for de-duplication, aggregatetype for the topic, aggregateid as key, type and payload; purpose to avoid inconsistencies between 'a service's internal state' and the events consumed.
evidence.shows: Shows the mechanism is documented and what each column is for.

transition_in.carries_over: The dual-write problem.
transition_in.introduces: The outbox that solves it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For listings the outbox gives three properties: the producer chooses the event shape, publication is at least once, and order follows commit order per listing.

evidence.what: ListingSold with a sale channel and price instead of status=4; the relay can publish a row twice; order holds when the relay keeps table order and keys by listing ID.
evidence.shows: Makes each property concrete for listing events.

transition_in.carries_over: How the outbox works.
transition_in.introduces: What it gives a listing producer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The outbox costs a write-path change in every producer and a table to clean up, which is why legacy systems usually start elsewhere.

transition_in.carries_over: The outbox's properties.
transition_in.introduces: Its cost, and the reason legacy systems need another path.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A monolith whose write paths are scattered cannot get an outbox quickly, so table-level change data capture, which turns every row change into an event without touching application code, is the strangler's first tool.

evidence.what: Kleinanzeigen's search team used Debezium on existing Kafka Connect clusters to stream MySQL changes into a denormalized per-user object on a compacted topic, up to 50,000 messages per second on full re-consumption, and found it harder to troubleshoot because issues 'often arise at the infrastructure level rather than in the application code'.
evidence.shows: Shows CDC working at classifieds scale, and its operational cost.

transition_in.carries_over: Legacy systems cannot take the outbox's write-path change quickly.
transition_in.introduces: Change data capture as the way to get events out of Yardstick.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A translator (an anti-corruption layer) is the only reader of the monolith's raw change events and emits the contract events, so that when the write path moves to a new service with its own outbox consumers do not notice, which makes CDC and outbox stages of one migration rather than alternatives.

evidence.what: Five mechanisms (publish after commit, polling, raw CDC, CDC plus translator, outbox) with what each guarantees, costs and when it is right.
evidence.shows: Places CDC plus translator as the migration stage and the outbox as the target.

evidence.what: When the write path leaves the monolith, the new service publishes the same contract through its own outbox and consumers do not notice; modernization-and-migration uses this sequence.
evidence.shows: Shows why the two are stages: consumers see one contract throughout.

transition_in.carries_over: CDC gets events out of a monolith without code changes.
transition_in.introduces: Why raw CDC still must not reach consumers, and the translator that stops it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every listing event shares one envelope whose fields are chosen for what consumers need to be correct: identity and key, version, timing, tenant, cause, correlation, schema, public state and the change.

evidence.what: Eleven fields: event_id, event_type, listing_id, listing_version, occurred_at/published_at, tenant, cause, correlation_id, schema_version, state, change, each with meaning and why consumers need it.
evidence.shows: Ties each field to a consumer need such as de-duplication, version-gated apply or per-tenant objectives.

evidence.what: Tenant glossed as one brand in one country, with a pointer to multi-country-platforms.
evidence.shows: Explains a term the reader meets here before the chapter that defines it.

transition_in.carries_over: How events are published, by outbox or translator.
transition_in.introduces: What every published event contains.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first of two envelope choices that need justification is that events carry both the delta and the full public state, so the alert matcher gets the price change it needs and a consumer that missed one event is repaired by the next: self-healing beats perfect delivery.

evidence.what: PriceChanged with old and new price in change and the listing in state; about 4 KB on average at Veldmark without media; a missed ListingUpdated version 7 repaired by PriceChanged version 8.
evidence.shows: Shows the cost of the larger event and what it buys.

transition_in.carries_over: The envelope's fields.
transition_in.introduces: The first of the two choices that need arguing: delta plus state.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second envelope choice is that the state block holds only public fields and what search and trust need, never seller contact data, which keeps personal data off the stream and shrinks the erasure problem.

evidence.what: The generic real-estate domain model: 'public fields can be published; draft, owner, and performance data remain internal and role-controlled'.
evidence.shows: Shows the same line drawn independently for a listing entity.

evidence.what: Consumers that need contact data fetch it through an access-controlled API at the moment of use; erasure belongs to listing-data-management.
evidence.shows: Says where contact data comes from instead and why that matters.

sections.heading: In Practice: Public Evidence and Contract v1

sections.heading: Schema Evolution
sections.controlling_idea: A listing schema with unknown consumers must evolve under full transitive compatibility, with changes in meaning reviewed by people and breaking changes made by parallel run.

advances_thesis.how: Says how the contract changes for years without breaking consumers.

flow.rationale: The modes before the choice of mode, since FULL_TRANSITIVE means nothing without them; the rules after the mode they implement; the change the rules cannot catch next; breaking changes last, after the rules that forbid them in place, since a parallel run is only needed for what the rules refuse.

transition_in.carries_over: The fourth design decision, FULL_TRANSITIVE compatibility, promised for this section.
transition_in.introduces: Why the contract needs it and how the schema changes over years.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing event schema lives for years with consumers its producers have never met, which makes changing it safely the chapter's hardest operational discipline.

Confluent Schema Registry offers backward, forward and full compatibility, each optionally transitive, which differ in whether new consumers read old data, old consumers read new data, or both, against the last version or all of them.

evidence.what: BACKWARD is the default and checked only against the latest version; transitive variants check all previous versions; FORWARD lets old consumers read new data; FULL means both; BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE recommended for Protobuf, a format the contract does not use.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the options the next paragraph chooses from.

transition_in.carries_over: Changing a long-lived schema safely.
transition_in.introduces: The compatibility modes a registry enforces.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A multi-brand listing stream needs full transitive compatibility because producers and consumers upgrade independently and replay old events, and in Avro that allows little beyond adding or removing optional fields with defaults, which is the point.

evidence.what: Any consumer, on any schema version, can read any event on the topic.
evidence.shows: Shows why independent upgrades and replay need both directions against all versions.

transition_in.carries_over: The compatibility modes.
transition_in.introduces: The one a multi-brand stream needs, and its consequence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A change of meaning is the dangerous one because a registry checks syntax, not semantics, so Veldmark routes every contract change through the advice forum's one-week event-catalog review.

evidence.what: Veldmark's rules: optional field yes; new event type with four weeks' notice; enum value only with a default branch (strings, not Avro enums); rename no; change of meaning never in place; remove a required field or change a type means a new major version.
evidence.shows: Turns full transitive compatibility into rules a producer can follow.

evidence.what: Hearthly sending surface_m2 as habitable instead of total surface passes every check and makes every valuation wrong.
evidence.shows: Shows a breaking change no registry detects.

transition_in.carries_over: Full transitive compatibility.
transition_in.introduces: Veldmark's published rules and the one change they cannot enforce by machine.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A breaking change means a new topic published in parallel until the consumer registry shows no v1 consumers, a deliberately high cost that keeps v2 rare; Veldmark expects v1 to last at least until Yardstick goes at the end of 2029.

evidence.what: listing.events.v2 with double publication; v1 retired when no active v1 consumer groups remain; v1 expected to last until Yardstick's decommissioning at the end of 2029.
evidence.shows: Shows how a breaking change is made and why it is rare.

transition_in.carries_over: Changes the rules allow or forbid in place.
transition_in.introduces: How a breaking change is made.

sections.heading: Replay, Backfills and Dead Letters
sections.controlling_idea: Replay, backfills and dead letters are designed so that no redelivered, backfilled or reprocessed event can bring a sold listing back.

advances_thesis.how: Shows how version gating and state-carrying events keep the stream safe on bad days and why removals are measured separately.

flow.rationale: Why replay matters, its sources, the backfill hazard and the version gate that solves it, Veldmark's backfill topic; then dead letters, a second hazard that reuses the version gate and the state-carrying event, so it must come after them. Dead letters first would explain the trap before the version gate that defuses it.

transition_in.carries_over: Schema evolution: changing the contract safely.
transition_in.introduces: Replaying its events safely.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing stream earns most of its value on bad days, when an index must be rebuilt, a new service bootstrapped or 300,000 wrong listings corrected, and each of these is a replay.

evidence.what: A search mapping change, a new recommendation service, an enrichment bug on 300,000 listings.
evidence.shows: Shows replay is routine work, not an exception.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three replay sources serve different purposes: the events topic for recent reprocessing, the compacted state topic for bootstrapping and rebuilds, and a backfill from the system of record for corrections.

evidence.what: Source, use and limit for each: 14-day retention; latest state only; load on the producer.
evidence.shows: Shows which source fits which replay.

transition_in.carries_over: The replays a stream must support.
transition_in.introduces: The sources they read from.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Backfills are where designs fail, because a backfilled event can overwrite a newer live one and resurrect a sold listing, and version-gated apply prevents it.

evidence.what: A backfilled ListingUpdated, read before the sale, processed after a live ListingSold; it carries the version at which it was read, not newer than the one applied, so it is ignored.
evidence.shows: Shows the hazard and how the version gate removes it.

transition_in.carries_over: The three sources.
transition_in.introduces: The one where designs fail.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vinted's merged reindex topic is documented without saying how stale batch events are kept from overwriting newer state, so the author infers that any such design needs a version or timestamp check in the consumer.

evidence.what: Vinted merged batch reindex events with organic changes on one topic.
evidence.shows: Shows a public design with the same hazard.

evidence.what: Figure 4: a version gate in front of a consumer holding v9 Sold, bouncing a duplicate v9 and a backfilled v7.
evidence.shows: Shows version-gated apply at a glance.

transition_in.carries_over: The backfill hazard and the version gate.
transition_in.introduces: A documented design where the safeguard is not stated, with the author's labelled inference.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark publishes backfills to a separate topic that consumers read at lower priority and gate by version, so the alert matcher can ignore old changes and a rebuild can be throttled without slowing live publication.

evidence.what: listing.backfill.v1, same schema, cause backfill.
evidence.shows: Shows the separation and what each consumer gains.

transition_in.carries_over: Backfills mixed with live changes on one topic.
transition_in.introduces: Veldmark's separate backfill topic.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A dead-letter queue holds events a consumer could not process, and for listings it hides a trap: reprocessing an old version from it without a version check overwrites newer state.

evidence.what: Version 5 in the dead-letter queue, version 6 processed, version 5 reprocessed later.
evidence.shows: Shows how a dead letter becomes a resurrection.

transition_in.carries_over: Backfills that overwrite newer state.
transition_in.introduces: Dead letters, which can do the same.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two rules defuse it: because events carry full state, skipping a failed one is usually safe, and consumers that need every delta park the failing listing while others continue.

evidence.what: Version 6 contains everything version 5 did; the price-drop alert matcher parks per key so one broken listing does not stop the partition.
evidence.shows: Shows how state transfer and per-key parking make dead letters safe.

transition_in.carries_over: The dead-letter trap.
transition_in.introduces: The two rules that handle it.

conclusion.heading: From Events to Copies
conclusion.synthesis: Reliable publication and safe consumption are two halves of one contract: the producer's half (one emitter, outbox or translator, key and version) makes every committed change one event in order, and the consumer's half (version-gated apply, state that heals, a separate backfill topic, a removal objective) makes sure no redelivery, replay or late batch undoes it; most listing incidents sit where one half is missing.
conclusion.so_what: A design with both halves catches the Sunday-peak, backfill and schema-change failures before buyers do, and lets a new consumer start without asking the producer.

callback.to: The hook: one listing written once and read by ten or twenty systems, and the scene's bike that a digest featured after it sold.
callback.how: The bike needed both halves: an event the digest heard, and a digest that re-checked state when it sent.

takeaway.content: Review the next listing event design by asking which half it is missing.

hand_off.carries_over: The stream moves changes and makes copies cheap, but it does not decide where the copies live, how stale each may be, or how an erasure reaches them.
hand_off.introduces: Listing data management: the system of record and the registered copies, shown on the same bike held in seven places.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Reliable publication and safe consumption are two halves that only work together, as the bike shows, so a design with both catches failures before buyers do and a review should begin by asking which half a design lacks.

evidence.what: The bike: ListingSold reaching the digest, and the digest re-checking state at send time.
evidence.shows: Calls back to the opening and shows both halves at work.

Presented CDC and outbox as stages (CDC behind a translator during migration, outbox as target) rather than alternatives, following the platform brief.
Kept behavioral tracking events off the listing stream and out of scope, to protect removal latency and keep data-platform's ownership clean.
Used the March 2027 bike digest incident as the motivating story and replayed it as v1's acceptance test, rather than inventing a new incident.

Converted spec.md's success criteria: the dual-write and CDC-as-source criteria became AC-4 (cold reader, minor); the schema-compatibility criterion became AC-5 (cold reader, minor); the evidence criterion became AC-6 (rubric, minor); the envelope and replay criteria are covered by the journal spec's AC-1; the ledger-match criterion was dropped (facts are governed by the scenario ledger, not by a reader outcome); the inventory criterion (tables, failure modes, view, questions) was dropped.

Added three units to the published text: lead-ins to the trade-off table (p54) and vertical table (p57) so each table is introduced and explained, and a synthesis paragraph (p68); merged the one-sentence signpost 'Two choices in the envelope deserve justification.' into p23 (flow rubric note) so the conclusion synthesizes and calls back to the opening rather than only handing off. Added a roadmap sentence to p03 (the journal spec's AC-2 asks the opening to predict the sections) and a one-clause gloss of 'tenant' to p21, since multi-country-platforms defines it later.
